p: Diego Silang y Andaya was born on 16 December 1730 in Aringay, then part of Pangasinan and now in La Union. His father was Pangasinense and his mother Ilocano. He was baptised on 7 January 1731 in Vigan, in the then undivided province of Ilocos, where as a boy he worked as a messenger for a local Castilian priest. Fluent in Spanish, he carried correspondence from the Ilocos to Manila, journeys on which he first saw the injustices of colonial rule.

Spain was allied with France in the Seven Years' War, and the British seizure of Manila in October 1762 inspired risings in the far north of Luzon. Silang at first wanted to replace Spanish functionaries in the Ilocos with native-born officials and offered to lead Ilocano forces on the Spanish side. The Spanish administrators instead transferred their powers to the Catholic Bishop of Nueva Segovia, who rejected the offer. The revolt drew on grievances over Spanish taxation and abuses and on Silang's belief that church and government in the Ilocos should be led by trained Ilocano officials.

Joaquín Martínez de Zúñiga, writing in 1805, gave a hostile account. He called Silang very quick and artful and said he persuaded the chiefs and many commoners, especially those of Vigan, that to keep the Catholic faith they must arm against the Spaniards and deliver them to the English. Armed men demanded that the alcalde give up his staff of government to the vicar-general; he did so and escaped from the province. The rebels then demanded of the bishop-elect, a Dominican named Ustariz, an exemption from the tribute, while Silang gathered troops for wider operations.

Silang was killed on 28 May 1763, aged 32, by a friend, a Spanish-Ilocano mestizo named Miguel Vicos, whom church authorities had paid and who was helped by Pedro Becbec. Gabriela Silang was forced to retreat to what is now Abra, led her troops towards Vigan and was driven back; she and her men were hanged on 20 September 1763, she last of all. The Philippine Navy has named two frigates after Diego Silang, one in service from 1976 to 1990 and one that entered service in 2025.

notes: A thin article: much of the revolt's course is known here only from the long quotation of Martínez de Zúñiga (1805), which I paraphrased and attributed. The article says nothing of who Zúñiga was, so he is named without a description; 'hostile' is my reading of the quotation's wording ('artful', 'specious arguments', 'seduced').
The article's dates are month-first; turned day-first.
The article does not mention the taking of Vigan in 1762 or the declaration of vassalage to the British that the existing description gives.
